newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's de Klerk meets Tutu on truth probe.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's de Klerk meets Tutu on truth probe.

text.p: South Africa's white-led National Party (NP) promised Archbishop Desmond Tutu's truth commission on Thursday it would answer questions within two weeks on its human rights record under apartheid.

NP leader F.W. de Klerk, who repudiated apartheid in 1990 and four years later surrendered power to President Nelson Mandela, a political prisoner for 27 years, said in a statement after talks with Tutu:
"The National Party will continue to cooperate with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission as long as we are treated justly."
De Klerk said he told Tutu there was a growing perception amongst his followers that the commission set up to heal the wounds of apartheid was prejudiced against some groups.
He said he told Tutu also that the police atrocities being revealed in truth commission hearings around the country were the work of a minority and were not endemic to the force.
De Klerk met Tutu, who recently recovered from surgery for prostate cancer, and his deputy, Alex Boraine, who last year slammed the NP's first submission to the truth commission.
The NP leader said the party would submit written answers within two weeks to questions put by the commission after his first appearance and would attend a further hearing within about two months.

Tutu said in a separate statement that de Klerk had asked for the meeting to discuss a controversial apartheid-era report on the role of the military in a government dirty-tricks campaign against Mandela's African National Congress.
The report, prepared in 1992 by General Pierre Steyn, a former South African military chief of staff, named more than 60 senior soldiers implicated in human rights abuses.

Tutu said the issue of the report was raised "very briefly" before De Klerk, South Africa's last white president, complained that the commission was not being even handed and was not placing enough emphasis on reconciliation.
"Dr Boraine and I reasured Mr de Klerk that the commission was totally committed to even-handedness and gave him a range of examples demonstrating this.
"We also sought to reassure him that reconciliation was our ultimate goal, although the commission could play only a small part in the long-term task of bringing it about," Tutu said.
